{{Short description|German physicist}}
'''Claus E. Rolfs''' (born 1941 in [[Bad Peterstal]]) is a German experimental physicist, known for his laboratory research related to nuclear astrophysics. He is a co-initiator of [[Nuclei in the Cosmos]].

==Biography==
Rolfs went to school in [[Offenburg]] and studied physics at the [[University of Freiburg]]. From 1973 he was a close associate of [[William A. Fowler]] at [[Caltech]], where Rolfs was a Millikan Fellow. In the 1970s and 1980s Rolfs was a professor at the [[University of Münster]]. He was a professor at the [[Ruhr University Bochum]] from 1990 to 2007, when he retired as professor emeritus. He lives in [[Münster]]. In 1980 he was a visiting professor at [[Ohio State University]].{{citation needed|date=September 2023}}

Rolfs has collaborated in many laboratory experiments that collect data on the nuclear fusion reactions that also take place in the [[Sun]].

Beginning in 2005 he considered radical, new ideas concerning the treatment of [[radioactive waste]]. In 2006 he and his team published the highly controversial indications of their experiments involving beta-decay.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Limata, B.|author2=Raiola, F.|author3=Wang, B.|author4=Yan, S.|author5=Becker, H.W.|author6=D'Onofrio, A.|author7=Gialanella, L.|author8=Roca, V.|author9=Rolfs, C.|author10=Romano, M.|author11=Schürmann, D.|year=2006|title=First hints on a change of the <sup>22</sup>Na βdecay half-life in the metal Pd|journal=The European Physical Journal A|volume=28|issue=2|pages=251–252|doi=10.1140/epja/i2006-10057-1 |bibcode=2006EPJA...28..251L |s2cid=123267830 }}</ref> Rolfs claimed that "by encasing certain radioisotopes in metal and chilling them close to absolute zero, it ought to be possible to slash their half-lives from millennia to just a few years."<ref>{{cite journal|title=Half-life heresy: Accelerating radioactive decay|date=18 October 2006|journal=New Scientist|url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg19225741-100-half-life-heresy-accelerating-radioactive-decay/}}</ref> However, the alleged change in half-life has been disconfirmed by subsequent experiments.<ref>{{cite book|title=Can environmental factors affect half-live in beta-decay? An analysis ''(doctoral dissertation, Texas A&M University)''|author=Goodwin, John Randall|date=December 2012|url=https://oaktrust.library.tamu.edu/bitstream/handle/1969.1/148338/GOODWIN-DISSERTATION-2012.pdf?sequence=1&isAllowed=y}}</ref> The uranium isotope ratios are also identical in various uranium ore deposits worldwide, indicating that, in the natural history of planet Earth, the half-lives of uranium's radioactive isotopes are significantly influenced by neither the temperature nor the chemical environment — although isotopic signatures can be affected by "reduction of uranium to [[Uranium dioxide|UO<sub>2</sub>]] or chemical precipitation in the form of U<sup>6+</sup> minerals."<ref>{{cite journal|author=Uvarova, Y.A.|author2=Kyser, T.K.|author3=Geagea, M.L.|author4=Chipley, D.|year=2014|title=Variations in the uranium isotopic compositions of uranium ores from different types of uranium deposits|journal=Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta|volume=146|pages=1–17|doi=10.1016/j.gca.2014.09.034 |bibcode=2014GeCoA.146....1U |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0016703714005924|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Rolfs is the author or co-author of over 450 articles and is also the author of several books in German for young people.

In 1972 he was the representative of Canada at the [[IAEA]] in Vienna. In 1979 he received the Roentgen Prize of the [[University of Gießen]]. He has several honorary doctorates ([[Naples]], [[Catania]], Lisbon). In 2006 he received the Saha Memorial Prize in Calcutta and in 1989 the Belgian-German Humboldt Prize. In 2010 he received the [[Hans A. Bethe Prize]] for "seminal contributions to the experimental determination of nuclear cross-sections in stars, including the first direct measurement of the key <sup>3</sup>He fusion reaction at solar conditions.".<ref>{{cite web|title=2010 Hans A. Bethe Prize Recipient, Claus Rolfs|website=American Physical Society|url=http://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Rolfs&first_nm=Claus&Year=2010}}</ref>

Rolfs plays several musical instruments.{{citation needed|date=September 2023}}

His doctoral students include [[Michael Wiescher]].{{citation needed|date=September 2023}}
